corrected_value.title: Girls’ comparative advantage in reading can largely explain the gender gap in math-related fields

decisions.quote:
Women remain underrepresented in most math-intensive fields. [Breda and Napp,
Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.
116
, 15435 (2019)] reported that girls’ comparative advantage in reading over math (i.e., the intraindividual differences between girls’ reading vs. math performance, compared to such differences for boys) could explain up to 80% of the gender gap in students’ intentions to pursue math-intensive studies and careers, in conflict with findings from previous research. We conducted a conceptual replication and expanded upon Breda and Napp’s study by using new global data (PISA2018,
N
= 466,165) and a recent US nationally representative longitudinal study (High School Longitudinal Study of 2009,
N
= 6,560).
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind target 0 identify Breda and Napp (2019) as the tested original study, resolving the conflicting_dois flag: the shipped row lists the SSRN working paper version (10.2139/ssrn.3435378), whereas the primary source explicitly cites and conceptually replicates the published PNAS article in Reference 4 (10.1073/pnas.1905779116, 'Girls’ comparative advantage in reading can largely explain the gender gap in math-related fields'). Per the codebook, the citation printed in the paper's reference list for the published article governs over a working paper.

decisions.reason: Across both new datasets (PISA2018 and HSLS:09), math-reading performance differences explained only a small fraction (0.4% to 12.3%) of the gender gap in math-intensive intentions and college major choices, compared to up to 80% in Breda and Napp (2019). Although the preliminary descriptive pattern that girls have a comparative advantage in reading held with smaller effect sizes, the authors state an explicit overall verdict that their finding contradicts Breda and Napp's main result.

decisions.reason: The study re-tests Breda and Napp's (2019) published finding (originally estimated on PISA2012 and a French high school cohort) using two different samples (PISA2018 and HSLS:09), which qualifies as a replication under the codebook.
